unit.title: Manage budgets and financial plans within the work team

summary: This unit teaches you to manage the budget and financial plan of a work team. You will learn to build a team financial plan from the work plan, cost activities and staff time, involve and brief the team, support financial procedures, monitor spending and variances, control and reduce costs, report problems early, and review how well the team managed its money.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. It teaches you to manage the **money of a work team**: to turn the team's work plan into a financial plan, cost its activities and staff, involve and brief the team, follow financial procedures, monitor spending against the plan, control and reduce costs, report problems early and review how well the team managed its money.

A team leader does not usually set the organisation's budget, but she is **answerable for how her team spends its share**. Team members also spend money every day: they order supplies, work overtime, claim expenses and use equipment. Good financial management at team level therefore depends on clear plans, clear procedures and a team that understands them.
**Who it is for:** team leaders and supervisors in businesses, hotels, schools, health centres and public bodies who hold a cost centre or a share of a department's budget.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Work from the work plan, cost each activity and each type of resource, and compare the total with the money allocated.
Ask staff for the real costs, explain the approved plan and say who is responsible for which costs.
Show staff how to raise purchase requests, claim expenses and follow approval limits, and apply the rules fairly.
Keep the team's own records, check them against the finance report and investigate variances.
Find savings with the team without harming service, and judge requests for new equipment.
Warn your manager early, with figures and options, and revise the plan when workload changes.
Judge how well the team managed its money and use the lessons for the next plan.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with scenarios and sums.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms and calculations) and longer answers.
**Practical group tasks**: preparing and briefing a team financial plan, and running a team cost-saving workshop and review of the team's financial processes.

blocks.note: Work every sum twice, and check the units. Many marks are lost by using the wrong base for a percentage or by forgetting a cost in a total.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **team financial plan** shows what resources the team's work needs, what they cost and when the money is needed. It is built from the team's **work plan** (targets, activities, staffing and deadlines), not the other way round. A financial plan that does not match the work plan puts money in the wrong places or at the wrong times.

flow: Start with the team's work plan and targets
List the activities and the resources each needs
Gather data on prices, usage and past costs
Work out the cost of each heading
Add the totals and compare with the money allocated
Set priorities if the plan is over the allocation
Agree the plan with your manager and finance staff

blocks.h: Cost headings for a typical team

head: Heading
Examples
Information to use
rows: Salaries, overtime, temporary cover, training, allowances
Rosters, pay rates, expected workload, leave
Stationery, printing, cleaning materials, spare parts
Recorded usage rates and expected workload
Quotes, service contracts, age of equipment
Venue, catering, materials for a workshop
A small sum held for costs that cannot be foreseen
A percentage of the budget (for example 5%) agreed with your manager

ul: Last year's actual costs and this year's figures to date
The team's expected workload (for example hotel room occupancy, number of applications)
Supplier quotes and current price lists
Staff, who know the real costs of the work
Your manager and the finance staff who support the team

blocks.p: **Base figures on recorded usage rates and expected workload, not on guesses.** A supplies budget that is always wrong usually means usage was guessed.

blocks.h: When the requests are more than the money

blocks.p: Rank the requests by **how much each helps the team meet its targets**. Fund the essential ones first, defer or drop the least useful, and say what you have left out and why.

ul: **Scenario planning**: plan for a best case, an expected case and a worst case level of work or cost.
**Contingency**: a small sum held back. If you may hold 5% of a J$3,000,000 team budget, that is J$150,000.
**Contingency plan**: decide in advance what to cut or delay if a risk happens (for example a large client order slips), and agree it with your manager.

blocks.note: A team financial plan should be revised whenever the work changes. If a new service will raise the team's workload by a third from next quarter, the plan must be revised and the change agreed with your manager.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Most team budgeting is arithmetic: **quantity × price**, added up. Work each sum twice and check that no heading has been left out.

Working
Result
rows: Saving over part of a year
J$15,000 a month from month 4 to month 12 = 9 months × 15,000

blocks.h: Cost per unit as a measure

blocks.p: **Cost per unit** (cost per order, per application, per guest) shows whether the team is using money **efficiently as workload changes**. A total that rises with volume may not be a problem. If total spending rises 15% but work rises 20%, cost per unit has fallen.

head: Tool
What it does
Example
rows: Compares what a proposal costs with what it gains
Do the benefits to the team's work outweigh the full cost?
A J$240,000 scanner that saves J$20,000 a month pays back in 12 months
The value of the next best use given up
Money spent on a scanner cannot be spent on training
Compare the **total** cost, including delivery, and the quality
One quote J$84,000 including delivery; another J$78,000 plus J$9,000 delivery = J$87,000

blocks.note: The cheapest quote is not always the best. If one supplier is J$90,000 cheaper but has no experience in the subject, weigh price against quality and the results you need.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: In a public agency, buying must follow the **public procurement rules** and give **value for money**: competitive quotes or tenders above set limits, no favourite suppliers, and records kept. A team cannot choose a supplier it likes without quotes because it will save time.

sections.title: Involving, briefing and supporting the team

head: Benefit of involving the team
Risk, and how to manage it
rows: Staff know the real costs of the work, so figures are more accurate
It takes time: set a short timetable
Staff are more likely to support the plan, so control is better
Unrealistic requests: rank every request against the targets
Staff see the effect of their choices, so there are fewer surprises
Confidential data: share only what each person needs

blocks.p: Involve people in ways that fit their roles: ask for usage figures and ideas, but keep authority over the final plan with the team leader and her manager.

ul: Explain the work plan and the money behind it, in plain terms.
Show the **limits** (what may be spent, by whom, on what).
Show who looks after each cost heading (a responsibilities chart).
Explain how spending will be tracked and how often you will report back.
Invite questions and note any that need follow-up.

blocks.p: A **cost centre** is a unit of an organisation, such as a team or department, to which costs are charged and for which a manager is answerable. Every team member should know which costs they are personally responsible for controlling, so that they can make sensible choices and spot problems early.
An example responsibilities chart (the limits and owners are set by each organisation):

head: Cost heading
Owner
Limit without approval
Reported
rows: Per job limit set by team

blocks.p: Staff may not know how to raise a purchase request or complete a claim. The team leader should **show the procedure, the forms and who approves them**, and, where claims are often returned for being incomplete, hold a short session on the rules and give a **checklist**.

ul: Explain **why** procedures exist (accuracy, control, protection of the team).
Apply them to everyone, including yourself.
Do not approve something that breaks the procedure because it 'will save time': explain why the procedure matters and help him follow it.
**Do not split a purchase** into smaller orders to stay under an approval limit.
Keep claims and receipts complete, accurate and on time.
If a supplier offers a personal benefit (such as a discount on a television) in return for continued business, **refuse and report** under the organisation's rules.
If you find that a team member has claimed for trips she did not make, **report it** and follow the organisation's procedure, keeping the facts confidential and not accusing anyone in public.
Never use the team's money or cards for private purposes.

blocks.note: Do not accuse or investigate alone. Report suspected fraud to the person named in the procedure, record the facts and keep them confidential.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Monitoring means comparing **actual spending with the plan** often enough to act while there is still time. A team leader should review spending **regularly, such as monthly**, using the finance report and the team's own records.

Keep a simple record of what the team has ordered, committed and spent. It lets you **check the finance report** and spot errors or missing items. Keep the record in a **secure, shared, controlled place**, not on one person's personal laptop, where it may be lost, changed or seen without control.
A **variance** is the difference between the plan and the actual figure. A variance that increases cost above plan is **adverse**. One that reduces cost below plan is **favourable**.

flow: Collect the finance report and the team's own record
Compare each heading with the plan to date
Mark variances, adverse and favourable
Ask: is it a real overspend, a timing difference or an error?
Find the cause with the team
Decide and record the action
Report to your manager if the problem is significant

blocks.p: **Timing differences** occur when spending falls in a different month from the plan (for example an annual licence paid early). **Errors** occur when finance has charged the wrong cost centre. Neither is a real overspend, but both must be sorted out.

If printing is well above the plan for two months running, **find out with the team why printing has risen** before deciding on action: a larger workload, a new client report, waste, or a change in practice.

Share a simple monthly chart or table at the team meeting and discuss it, so that members see how the team is doing against its cost plan and how their choices affect it. People take responsibility when they understand the plan and see the effect of their choices.

A spreadsheet of planned and actual costs by month is most useful when it uses **formulas**, instructions that work out values automatically, such as the difference between plan and actual and the total to date. Protect the file, back it up, and keep one master copy.

blocks.note: A rising total is not always a problem. If workload rose 20% and cost per item fell, the team is more efficient even though it spent more. Always read variances beside activity.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: When asked to cut costs, for example by 8% for the rest of the year, the team leader should **work with the team** rather than impose cuts, and test every idea against its effect on service and staff.

flow: Say what has to be saved, by when, and what must not be harmed
Look at where the money goes (spend by heading)
Ask the team for ideas and note the estimated saving of each
Test each idea against its effect on service, safety and staff
Choose the best, with an owner and a date
Track the savings in the monthly report
Thank the team and report the result

head: Idea
Estimate
Check
rows: Move reports from paper to screens
Do all readers have screens? Any legal need for paper?
Plan rosters around the busy days shown by the records
Is cover enough on busy days? Are staff willing?
Storage, shelf life, cash tied up

blocks.p: If overtime keeps rising because work arrives unevenly, the best action is usually to **plan rosters around the busy days that the records show**, not to ban overtime or hire extra permanent staff without looking at the pattern.

The key question when judging a request for equipment is: **do the benefits to the team's work outweigh the full cost?** Include purchase, installation, training and maintenance. A J$210,000 scanner that saves J$14,000 a month pays back in 210,000 ÷ 14,000 = 15 months. If only six months of the year remain, it will not save money this year, but may still be worthwhile over its life.

blocks.note: Never save money by removing safety checks, ignoring legal duties or dropping quality. Find the savings elsewhere.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: When a team's suggestion, such as a way of cutting photocopier costs, works, **thank the team, report the saving, and say who suggested it**. Recognition keeps ideas coming.

sections.title: Reporting problems, revising the plan and reviewing the year

blocks.p: If a price rise will push the team over its plan, **tell your manager early**, with the figures and the options to cover it. Do not wait until the year-end.

head: A note to your manager should include
Example
rows: A supplier price rise from June
About J$200,000 over the plan by year end
Defer a purchase of J$120,000 and reduce printing by J$80,000; ask for advice on the rest

ul: Revise the plan when workload, prices or staffing change.
Agree revisions with your manager and finance.
Brief the team on what has changed.
Keep a record of the original and revised plan.

blocks.p: If the team will be under its plan at year end because a post was vacant for four months, **report this early** so that the money can be used well elsewhere. An underspend caused by a vacancy is not an efficiency saving: the work still had to be done, perhaps by overtime or at lower service.
At year end, ask: **did the team meet its targets within the plan, and were its forecasts accurate?** Look at each heading, the reasons for variances, and the effect on service and staff.

Write down what worked and what did not so that **next year's plan and procedures can be improved**. If supplies were always wrong because usage was guessed, base next year's figures on recorded usage and expected workload.

blocks.note: Share the lessons with your team and your manager, and thank people for their part. Teams that see their effort recognised take more care of the money.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: build a team financial plan from the team's work plan and compare it with the allocation
cost staff time, overtime, supplies and events, and work out totals, shares and cost per unit
rank requests when they are more than the money and plan for best, expected and worst cases
hold a contingency and agree a contingency plan with my manager
involve the team in planning and brief them on the approved plan and their responsibilities
show staff how to raise purchase requests and claims, and refuse requests that break the rules
report fraud, gifts and conflicts properly and keep the facts confidential
keep the team's own records, compare them with the finance report and explain variances
work out payback, savings and percentage variances
find savings with the team without harming service or safety
warn my manager early with the cause, amount, effect and proposed action
review the year and use the lessons next time

c1.title: A training day for a Montego Bay regional office
c1.text: The administration team of a government agency's regional office in Montego Bay will hold a one-day training workshop for 48 staff. Venue hire is J$150,000, lunch costs J$2,200 per person and materials cost J$38,000. The team has been allocated J$300,000 for the event. The organiser, Mrs Brown, hears that 8 more staff may ask to attend.

c2.title: Overtime in a Lucea hardware wholesaler's accounts office
c2.text: The accounts office of a wholesaler in Lucea plans 6 staff to work 5 hours of overtime each in a typical month, at J$1,350 an hour. In the latest month, 40 hours of overtime were worked at the same rate. The supervisor, Mr Taylor, notes from the time records that most extra hours fall on the first and last working days of the month, when invoices and statements are due.

c3.title: A health centre's administration team in Black River
c3.text: The administration team at a health centre in Black River has an annual plan of J$2,400,000 for consumables and travel, spread evenly: J$1,200,000 for the first six months. Actual spending for the half-year was J$1,380,000. The team had planned to process 5,000 patient forms in the half-year but processed 6,000. Printing was planned at J$150,000 and cost J$270,000. The finance report also shows a printing charge of J$45,000 that the team's own record does not contain.

c4.title: Cutting costs by 8% in a Kingston public agency
c4.text: A team of ten in a public agency in Kingston has J$2,500,000 left to spend this year and is asked to cut costs by 8% without harming service. Staff suggest moving reports from paper to screens, which would save 3,000 pages a month at J$10 a page for the six remaining months. Another suggestion is a J$210,000 scanner that would save J$14,000 a month. Two suppliers quote for new office chairs: Supplier A at J$84,000 including delivery, and Supplier B at J$78,000 plus J$9,000 delivery. A clerk also proposes splitting a J$120,000 purchase into three orders of J$40,000 to avoid the approval limit of J$50,000.

c5.title: A school administration team's year-end review in Clarendon
c5.text: The administration team of a secondary school in Clarendon had an annual budget of J$6,000,000 and spent J$5,520,000. A clerk's post, costing J$105,000 a month, was vacant for four months. The supplies forecast was J$300,000 and the actual cost was J$345,000. All service targets were met, although several staff worked extra hours to cover the vacancy. The team leader, Mr Scott, must write the review for the principal.

questions.q: What is the total cost of the workshop for 48 staff?
questions.why: Lunch = 48 × J$2,200 = J$105,600. Total = 150,000 + 105,600 + 38,000 = J$293,600. Each wrong figure leaves out one or more of the three costs.

questions.q: How much of the J$300,000 allocation is left after the planned cost?
questions.why: 300,000 − 293,600 = J$6,400. The margin is only about 2% of the allocation, so any extra cost will cause an overspend.

questions.q: If 8 more staff attend, by how much will the cost exceed the allocation?
questions.why: Lunch for 56 = 56 × 2,200 = J$123,200. Total = 150,000 + 123,200 + 38,000 = J$311,200, which is J$11,200 over J$300,000. J$17,600 is only the extra lunch cost.

questions.q: What is the best way for Mrs Brown to manage this risk?
o: Wait to see how many arrive and then ask for more money
Fix the number of places in advance, or ask early for a contingency
Reduce lunches for everyone to J$1,500 each
Cancel the workshop
questions.why: Managing risk means setting limits (a registration list) or agreeing in advance how extra cost will be met. Waiting until after the event leaves no time to act, and cutting quality for everyone is a poor remedy.

questions.q: What was the overtime plan for a typical month?
questions.why: 6 staff × 5 hours × J$1,350 = 30 hours × 1,350 = J$40,500. J$54,000 is the actual cost (40 hours).

questions.q: What is the variance in the latest month and how should it be described?
o: J$13,500 favourable
J$54,000 adverse
J$40,500 favourable
J$13,500 adverse
questions.why: Actual 40 × 1,350 = J$54,000. Variance = 54,000 − 40,500 = J$13,500 over plan, which is adverse. It is one third (33%) of the plan.

questions.q: What should Mr Taylor do first about the overtime?
o: Look at the time records by day and reason before acting
Ban all overtime from next month
Ask the finance department to increase the plan
Tell staff they must reduce their hours
questions.why: The records show the pattern: the extra hours cluster at month-end. Understanding the cause lets him plan rosters or work flow to suit. Banning overtime without checking could miss deadlines.

questions.q: What is the total variance for the half-year, and how is it described?
o: J$180,000 favourable
J$1,380,000 adverse
J$180,000 adverse
J$120,000 adverse
questions.why: 1,380,000 − 1,200,000 = J$180,000 over the plan. Spending above plan is an adverse variance. J$120,000 is only the printing overspend.

questions.q: By what percentage was printing over its plan?
questions.why: Printing variance = 270,000 − 150,000 = J$120,000. 120,000 ÷ 150,000 × 100 = 80% over plan. Dividing by the actual figure would give 44%.

questions.q: The plan was for 5,000 forms and 6,000 were processed. What does the cost per form show?
o: Cost per form fell from J$240 to J$230
Cost per form rose because the total rose
Cost per form is unchanged at J$240
Cost per form cannot be calculated
questions.why: Planned cost per form = 1,200,000 ÷ 5,000 = J$240. Actual = 1,380,000 ÷ 6,000 = J$230. The team spent more in total but each form cost less, so the overspend is partly the effect of higher workload.

questions.q: The finance report shows a J$45,000 printing charge that is not in the team's record. What should the team leader do?
o: Ignore it, because the team did not order it
Ask finance to delete it from the report
Deduct it from next month's printing figure
Check it with finance and update the team's record
questions.why: Differences between the finance report and the team's record may be an error, a missing record or a timing difference. Checking the invoice and the delivery is the only safe way to find out which.

questions.q: What is the saving from moving to screens over the six months, and how far does it go to the target?
o: J$30,000, leaving J$170,000 to find
J$180,000, leaving J$20,000 to find
J$200,000, meeting the target
J$18,000, leaving J$182,000 to find

questions.q: Which supplier is cheaper once delivery is included?
o: Supplier B, by J$6,000
Supplier A, by J$3,000
Supplier B, by J$3,000
They cost the same
questions.why: A = J$84,000. B = 78,000 + 9,000 = J$87,000. Compare total cost, including delivery, and then check quality and service.

questions.q: How long would the scanner take to pay for itself, and what does that mean this year?
o: 12 months, so it will save money this year
6 months, so it will meet the target
21 months, so it should be rejected
15 months, so no net saving this year
questions.why: 210,000 ÷ 14,000 = 15 months. Only six months remain, so the scanner adds cost this year. It might still be good value over its life, which is a separate judgement.

questions.q: What should the team leader say about splitting the J$120,000 purchase into three orders?
o: Refuse, and explain why limits must not be avoided
Allow it, because the total cost stays the same
Allow it, but record it as three separate items
Allow it once, if the supplier agrees to it
questions.why: Splitting a purchase to stay under an approval limit defeats the control and is a breach of procedure, and in a public body it also breaches procurement rules. Seek the right approval or quotes.

questions.q: What is the best way to find the savings the team needs?
o: Cut every heading by 8% without any discussion
Stop all spending on supplies and printing now
Ask the team for ideas, and test them against service
Cut the staff training budget and nothing else
questions.why: Team ideas are more likely to be practical and supported, and testing against service prevents savings that cause harm. Across-the-board cuts or stopping supplies may damage work.

questions.q: By what percentage was the team under its annual budget?
What share of the underspend came from the vacant post?
How should Mr Scott treat the underspend from the vacancy in his review?
o: As proof that the team can manage with fewer staff
As a saving to be taken from next year's budget
As a mistake in the finance department's report
As caused by the vacancy, with the extra hours noted
questions.why: The work still had to be done, and staff worked extra hours, so the underspend does not show better efficiency. An honest review reports the cause and the effect on staff and service.

questions.q: The supplies forecast was J$300,000 and the actual cost J$345,000. What did the forecast get wrong, and what should be done?
o: 15% too high; cut the supplies heading
15% too low; use recorded usage next year
13% too low; treat it as a one-off
45% too low; ask for a larger budget now
questions.why: (345,000 − 300,000) ÷ 300,000 = 15% over the forecast. A reliable forecast uses recorded usage rates and the expected workload, not a guess.
